What the parliament of Canada has chosen is that the Bank of Canada should have independent responsibility.
Read on what he said.
Mr. Speaker, I wonder whether the minister would now permit a question on the quotation he has given?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, but I wish to say that if there are any more of these observations and interjections from the Leader of the Opposition or the hon. member for Essex East from their seats in the house, they will be replied to, and suitably. But you see what happens? It is the same old thing. They are very touchy. Yesterday they would not have interruptions. They would not have questions, even when members were asking merely for an explanation. But now, when the shoe is on the other foot, there they sit. They are close to Hansard. The Leader of the Opposition gets off these wisecracks. It is debate by wisecrack as far as he is concerned, and then he goes on to lard up the record. If that is the way we are going to have the rules observed, then very well, but they must be evenly applied.

On a point of order. I have had the opportunity of looking at Hansard, that is quite true; but I have ascertained from Hansard that the minister himself made 24 interruptions when I spoke yesterday in an hour and ten minutes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think the Leader of the Opposition, if he is fair, will agree-
Yes, some of them were legitimate.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: All right. We will say no more about that, because the Leader of the Opposition did yield the floor on occasion yesterday, as I have always done when the hon. gentleman has sought to ask questions, and I propose to continue to do so. Did the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Mcllraith) wish to intervene?

I wanted to ask a question, but I am afraid we have been diverted. When the minister was quoting from the evidence given to the committee in 1954 he ended his quotation with the words: "There is no alibi possible for the central bank." Does the minister not think it would have been only fair to the house to have quoted the next sentence which has a direct bearing on the point?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I went on to stress twice the point in the next sentence and the next paragraph. I laid great stress on that. If the hon. member for Ottawa West cannot read

Government Monetary Policy this next sentence I shall be glad to read it for him, but it will not go one inch further:
On the other hand, there is no alibi possible for the government, because if government said: well, we disagreed with what the central bank did, but parliament has placed the responsibility on them, so what could we do? The answer obviously is that the administration of the day, supported by a majority in parliament, can always alter the legislation.
I quoted those words, and that is precisely what I said. The administration of the day, supported by a majority in parliament, could always alter the legislation.

That is not the
whole picture, and you know it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It was the whole picture that Mr. Graham Towers put before the committee. With all respect to the supernatural omniscience of the hon. member for Essex East, I still prefer Mr. Graham Towers speaking with authority on the subject of the Bank of Canada. That will point very clearly to the fact that the government as such has no power to exercise over the Bank of Canada. It rests with parliament. Parliament can always alter the legislation. But short of that, the bank in these matters has the responsibility. That is the effect of the legislation enacted by this parliament as it has been in effect for many years.
Now I proceed to 1956. That was a very interesting time indeed, because there had been a good deal of debate on the subject of tight money, and the government had been holding back on that subject. Finally, on August 10 and 11, the minister of finance of that day was really cornered and we began to elicit from him some statements which have made very interesting reading since. The reference made yesterday to this subject by the Leader of the Opposition was highly selective. He chose to read his extracts from August 11, 1956. He did not choose to deal with what was said on the same subject on August 10, the day before. So I am going to refresh his memory. At page 7351 of Hansard of August 10, the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe) who at that time was acting leader of the opposition pressed certain questions on the orders of the day, and on his second try he got this statement out of Mr. Harris, then minister of finance. The discussion at that time revolved around an increase made by the bank in the bank rate. Mr. Harris said:
The duty of the Bank of Canada is to regulate the interest rate, which is commonly known as the bank rate. That duty and responsibility is imposed upon the bank and not upon the government, and it has not been customary in the past for any minister of finance to comment on the actions of the bank in discharging its duty. As a matter of fact, however, without admitting some of the opinions or facts that have been stated in

the question, 1 may say that there is a considerable body of opinion in the financial world today that unless action of this kind were taken there might be more serious results than if no action were taken.
Then the minister was pressed further by the present Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) and he replied:
I answered this question some two months ago by saying that the governor of the Bank of Canada is one of the several advisors to the minister of finance. In this particular matter, however-
That is, the determination of the bank rate.
-he has statutory authority to make his own decisions, that statutory authority having been conferred upon him by parliament. I think it would be correct to say, as I said on the former occasion, that I was advised of this course before it was taken.
That is the point. He was advised. That is where the responsibility of the government comes in.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I presume that even the hon. member for Essex East may have been advised, too, Mr. Speaker. But he was advised of what the governor of the bank intended to do in exercise of the authority conferred upon him.
To make sure it was not contrary to government policy.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The babbling brook goes on forever.

Insults do not enrich your argument. All the hon. gentleman can do is add personal insult. Let him deal with this thing on its merits. The fact is that the governor of the Bank of Canada did seek the advice of those who have final and legitimate responsibility for government in this country.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: You see, Mr. Speaker, the hon. member did not rise to ask a question. He did not ask me to yield the floor. He just stood up and proceeded to make a speech. That is an interesting commentary on his conception of the application of the rules of the house. They are binding on 264 members, but this exalted member is above all the rules of the house.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: You should have been around last night to see how well they were observed.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No doubt the same thing happened then. The hon. member has undertaken to say, presumably on his own authority, that the government was consulted and apparently took some responsibility in relation to approval. That is not what his former colleague, the minister of finance, said. The then minister of finance was pointing out that he was acquainted in advance of what the bank was going to do in the exercise of

its own statutory power and responsibility. May I now refresh the failing memory of the hon. member for Essex East because, you see, the hon. member has made another blunder; he has put his foot in it again.
There then followed this question from the present Prime Minister:
Did the minister in any way suggest, having regard to the inflationary tendencies in this country today, that this action should be taken or might be taken by the bank?
To which Mr. Harris replied:
I also answered that question two months ago by saying that this action is the action of the governor of the bank and his responsibility alone.
So, on the facts, you have to make your choice between the hon. member for Essex East, speaking now, some five years after this event with his usual irresponsibility and the minister of finance of that time speaking on August 10, 1956, because the statements made today by the hon. member for Essex East and by the minister of finance in 1956 are completely contradictory.

I was going to ask the minister if he is not aware that, while there is no question about the bank being responsible for policy action, in the evidence to which he has just referred-a part which the hon. gentleman did not read-the statement is made that if action by the bank was in conflict with the policy of the government, the governor would resign.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The Leader of the Opposition has pointed out to us that it is only parliament and not the government that has power in this respect in relation to the resignation of anybody, whether governor or bank directors, but the hon. gentleman is wrong again. I have not finished reading this. It is regrettable that hon. members opposite only read Hansard, of August 11 and do not look back at August 10. It is a selective habit they have.
As reported at page 7352 of Hansard of August 10, the then hon. member for Rose-town-Biggar, Mr. Coldwell, asked this question:
While it is true that the governor of the Bank of Canada makes the Anal decision in these matters, is it not a fact that the Bank of Canada was established In order that it might control the economy and carry out government policy in that particular? Is it not a fact that was the main reason for its establishment?
Let me interject here, Mr. Speaker, that had those questions been put to the Leader of the Opposition yesterday he would, of course, have answered yes to both questions.

Nonsense.
Government Monetary Policy

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
But observe the answer of Mr. Harris:
I do not think that is a correct interpretation of the statute,-
That is right.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I continue:
-though anyone can put such an interpretation on it if he so desires. I think the purpose was not only to vest ownership of the bank in the government, as has been done, but to vest in the officials of the bank independent authority-
Under government policy.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
He did not say that.
He said, "independent authority".
Well, that is obvious.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The Leader of the Opposition has no right whatever to add qualifications to the statement made by the hon. Walter Harris in this house in 1956. Mr. Harris was quite capable of making his own statements and it is not within the right of the Leader of the Opposition or any other hon. member of this house now to qualify or contradict by qualification the plain statement made on that occasion by the then minister of finance.
The discussion proceeded further and the then prime minister, Mr. St. Laurent, was brought into the discussion. The present Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton) asked this question:
Does the Prime Minister know the reason for
the increase in the rate and, if so, does he agree that it is necessary?
The then prime minister, Mr. St. Laurent, replied:
The Prime Minister is not the governor of the Bank of Canada, and while I hope that if he were perhaps the hon. gentleman would have more confidence in his decision than in the decision of the present staff, 1 can assure the hon. gentleman that the matter received very serious consideration and the government has not decided to recommended to parliament any amendment to the act which places that responsibility on the governor of the Bank of Canada.
That is right.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, that certainly is right and it completely contradicts the assertions made here yesterday by the Leader of the Opposition and volubly supported from a seated position by the hon. member for Essex East.

Do not be so narrow and
legalistic.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The present Prime Minister then directed a question to Mr. St. Laurent in these words:
Will the Prime Minister, having had the reasons from the governor of the Bank of Canada, now give the house the benefit of what those reasons were?

Government Monetary Policy
In reply to that question the then prime *minister said:
No, Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister will not undertake to have parliament or the members of the opposition act as a court of appeal from the decision made by the governor of the Bank of Canada-
Then there were cries of "Oh, oh," and the then prime minister added:

unless and until parliament amends the act which now governs the Bank of Canada.
Mr. Speaker, it is too bad that hon. members opposite have sought in this debate to pull the rug out from under the feet of Mr. St. Laurent, but Mr. St. Laurent's statement is there on the record. It is clear, it is incontestable and it stands as a statement of the effect and meaning and proper construction of the provisions of the Bank of Canada Act. It is not open to challenge by any hon. member opposite.
It has been challenged by the Minister of Finance.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No, not at all, Mr. Speaker. Mr. St. Laurent was plainly saying what I have contended in this respect and was also contradicting in the plainest terms the kind of specious but utterly empty and inane arguments put forward yesterday by the Leader of the Opposition.
The Leader of the Opposition referred yesterday to the debate which proceeded on August 11 and quoted a statement which I made in that debate. Let me make it very clear that if I had ever foreseen at that time that my remark was going to be wrenched and distorted in the way in which the Leader of the Opposition has sought to bend it out of recognition to serve his argument yesterday, it would never have been said in those terms.
I made my statement with reference to over-all financial policy in Canada. I do not think there is anything in that statement which ought to be interpreted as supporting the thesis put forward by the Leader of the Opposition yesterday that under the provisions enacted by parliament with respect to the Bank of Canada Act, the government has power to direct the Bank of Canada or to call upon the Bank of Canada to observe a position of responsibility to the government as such, rather than to parliament. The Bank of Canada, of course, has its responsibility to parliament.
Read the speech.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I have dwelt on that subject at some length. It was read yesterday by the Leader of the Opposition and referred to again today and I have made my own comment on it in what I think are plain and understandable terms.


From the time Mr. St. Laurent made his comment on the effect of the language of the act in 1956 until the present, the situation has not altered. The act has not been amended. Parliament has not seen fit to amend the provisions of the act and the matter stands there in the position in which Mr. St. Laurent described it in 1956. It is the legislation enacted by parliament that governs the relationships in this matter.
Will my hon. friend permit a question?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I refer, of course to the relationships between parliament, the government and the Bank of Canada. The decisions that are made in this situation are those of the governor and those of the bank and are not those of the government.
Will my hon. friend permit a question?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, now.
I am seriously trying-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Let us have the question.

-to arrive at my hon. friend's position and to fully understand it. Does the hon. gentleman agree with the statement that was made by one of his own predecessors, Mr. Ilsley, who when speaking of a possible disagreement between the bank and the government said in this house in 1941 that in the event of a disagreement between the Bank of Canada and the government:
-it would be necessary for them-
That is, the bank. I continue:
*-to resign, and they would be replaced by others who were willing to accept the responsibility for the type of policy which the government believed to be appropriate.
Does my hon. friend agree with that statement made by a former distinguished minister of finance?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, no, not in those terms. Not at all.
We do.
That is the issue.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Unless, in the event of disagreement, the governor and the directors chose to resign there is nothing the government is in a position to do in that situation except to ask parliament to change the legislation or wait for the expiry of their terms because, as the Leader of the Opposition said yesterday, referring to the governor

and the directors-I repeat once more-"they can be removed only by parliament." That was a direct statement.

Would the hon. gentleman permit a question? This is a very critical and important matter. I would ask the minister, then, in this situation, does he believe the governor of the bank can do or say what he likes in this field and that the government can do nothing about it?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Let us take the extreme case of a headlong clash, Mr. Speaker. In a situation of that nature the government would have no power whatever to terminate the terms of office of the directors or the governor. In that situation all it could do would be to go to parliament, as the Leader of the Opposition said yesterday in effect. That is all it could do. The government has not been given by parliament any power or authority over the bank or its senior officials or directors in that situation.
Let me now make some comments on the subject of money supply. Here again, the Leader of the Opposition drew a very long bow. Money supply consists of the total of issued currency and chartered bank deposits. May I remind the house of those words which I read from the Bank of Canada Act, that the bank has the sole right to issue notes payable to bearer on demand and intended for circulation in Canada. That is the effect of section 21. Nothing could be plainer. Parliament has emphasized that the Bank of Canada has the sole right in this matter. The bank alone determines what currency shall be issued and in this respect the legislative position is just as it was under the former Liberal administration.
The government has no voice whatever in this matter of money supply. Consequently, in whatever the Leader of the Opposition had to say yesterday by way of criticism in relation to money supply, those are matters over which the government has no control and whether or not the hon. gentleman realizes it-I think he must realize it-his criticisms were directed at the Bank of Canada and not at the government. The government has no power to add to or subtract from or change this money supply or currency that the Bank of Canada is given the sole power to create.
The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) had something to say yesterday about the increase in money supply from April to October, 1958. I am not going to dwell on this subject but his criticism, if valid, was quite misdirected. He said that the increase in money supply during that period was the largest monetary expansion since world war II. It was in fact $1.4 billion not adjusted for
Government Monetary Policy seasonal factors. The increase for the whole year 1958, that is, from the end of December, 1957, to the end of December, 1958, was $1,324 billion or 11.1 per cent. It is customary, Mr. Speaker, to measure the increase by comparison of dates a year apart.
The Leader of the Opposition then went on to attribute to the government's debt management policies all of this increase in money supply and he said it was "too large for the needs and stability of the economy". May I remind you, Mr. Speaker, that between the end of December, 1954, and the end of December, 1955, when he was a minister of the government, the money supply was increased by 10.5 per cent despite the lack of any comparable conversion loan and, indeed, in the face of a net retirement of government bonds of over $300 million. But I realize, Mr. Speaker, that the interesting occurrence, which I should like to put alongside what the Leader of the Opposition said yesterday, took place before Mr. Harris denied responsibility for monetary policy.
The Leader of the Opposition also referred to the reduction of $300 million in money supply between October, 1958, and May, 1960, as "more severe than in 1956". He then spoke of the money supply from April, 1960, to August, 1960, only four months, as having been kept "almost stable". The fact is that it increased $117 million in those four months.
As to the adequacy of money supply, Mr. Speaker, the house will have to be the judge of that. For the information of the house on this point I simply draw attention to the extent of increase in money supply at the end of 1960 compared with the end of 1959. Here I give the extent of increase or decrease in various countries taking the money supply at the end of 1959 as 100:
United States	 99
United Kingdom	 99
Sweden	 594
Australia	 194
Canada	 495
Germany	 497
The Netherlands	 197
Switzerland	 199
At December 31, 1960, the money supply in Canada was substantially larger than it had ever been before. I will just give the figures at the year end in the following years:

The figure at December 31, 1960, is by far the largest on record and it is 5.5 per cent higher than the corresponding figure at the end of 1959.
Yesterday the Leader of the Opposition made complaint about the striking of the bank rate.

Before the minister leaves these figures, I think he said that the figure at the end of December, 1960, was by far the largest. I take it he meant the largest compared with the same date in the previous year.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Oh, it is away higher than any previous date. The money supply moved up steadily in the second half of 1960.
It was higher a month earlier, for instance.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There are bound to be fluctuations from week to week.
What I wanted to get was that the minister's figures were all based on comparable dates in previous years.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes, and if the hon. member will compare the November, 1960, figure with the November, 1959, figure he will find a similar increase over the 1959 figure.
Yesterday the Leader of the Opposition talked about the bank rate. Again, Mr. Speaker, I emphasize that the determination of the bank rate is the responsibility of the Bank of Canada. The government has nothing whatever to do with it, and that was recognized by Mr. Harris. I give the reference, 1956 Hansard, page 7351.
It was on November 1, 1956, that the Bank of Canada adopted what has come to be known as the floating rate. It was a decision of the Bank of Canada and the Leader of the Opposition has criticized that decision. He criticized it in the face of the very plain terms of section 18, subsection 3, of the Bank of Canada Act. I quote:
The Bank shall at all times make public the minimum rate at which it is prepared to make loans or advances.
Mr. Harris said in the reference I have just made that it is the bank that determines the bank rate. The government has no control whatever over the rate that the bank sets or over the method it chooses by which to set this rate. If the Leader of the Opposition disapproved of this so-called floating rate, the rate attached by decision of the Bank of Canada to the 91-day treasury bill rate, then he had something like eight months in office to do something about it and he did not do anything about it. It was in his day

as a minister that this floating rate was adopted by the Bank of Canada.
I say that the government has no power whatsoever to interfere with the action of the bank in determining this rate or in choosing the method by which it shall determine the rate.
The Leader of the Opposition chose yesterday to make reference to what happened on August 20, 1959, and he described it as an interference with monetary policy on my part. That statement will bear some examination, Mr. Speaker. Here are the words of the Leader of the Opposition as found on page 2202 of Hansard:
After all, the minister and the government did not hesitate to interfere with the operations of monetary policy by the bank, so they should not attempt to evade responsibility for policy-
When this fell on my astounded ears I asked:
Mr. Speaker, to what is the Leader of the Opposition referring?
He then said:
I am thinking of the intervention of the government in the bank auction of treasury bills some time ago, which had an influence on the rate on treasury bills. The minister knows all about it. He knows all about the cabinet meeting which was held and the auction being postponed an hour or two so the government could make up its mind what to do.
It is on this statement that the Leader of the Opposition accuses the government and accuses me of interfering with the operations of monetary policy by the bank. I give to his assertion, Mr. Speaker, an unqualified contradiction. There was on that occasion not the slightest interference with the bank's monetary policy. Since this government came into office there has never been the slightest interference with the bank's monetary policy.
What happened on August 20, 1959, was that a decision was taken, and I take full responsibility for it, that the government would not sell all of the treasury bills for which it had invited tenders on that particular Thursday because I thought that the prices being offered were unsuitable. In effect, the discount that was applied at that time was, I thought, too high, and I was not prepared under those circumstances to have the government of Canada pay that high a price for 91-day treasury bill money. It was a decision in relation to the price the government was prepared to pay on its own borrowings on the 91-day treasury bills. That is what it was. It was not done with a view to affecting the bank rate at all. It was not, as the Leader of the Opposition says, an interference with monetary policy. It was open to the bank at that time to strike the rate at anything it decided upon. It was open to the bank to detach its rate from the

treasury bill rate. The purpose of this decision, which I made over in the Bank of Canada office when we saw what the bids were, was in relation to the price on these treasury bills. That was its entire purpose. Whatever bearing this may have had on the Bank of Canada rate for that week was entirely incidental; that was something that the Bank of Canada could set or change in any way it chose. There was on that occasion, and on all other occasions, no interference with the bank or with the bank rate.
Mr. Speaker, one could go on dealing with this subject and others related to it at some considerable length, but it seems to me that the essential issue here is this question of responsibility. Therefore I will pass over some intervening remarks that I had intended to make and take up what the Leader of the Opposition undertook to say about the interest rates. Here he was much less definite; much less effusive than he was in his unfounded assertions about the responsibility in relation to decisions of the Bank of Canada within the scope of monetary policy. He was seeking evidently to argue that the government in some way had raised interest rates. I wish again to make firm contradiction of any such statement. As long as the present government is in office you may be sure it is not going to pay one cent more interest on the moneys that it has to borrow than is strictly necessary. Interest rates are determined in this country-in this free economy -in the light of thousands of transactions. It is a matter of the operation of the forces of supply and demand within quite limited statutory restrictions. The situation in this regard is precisely the same as it was when the former government was in office.
If there has been a fluctuation in the interest rates, Mr. Speaker, I can only say that interest rates are constantly fluctuating; they had risen steadily for two years before we came into office. The rise was substantial, and the consequent drop in market values of issued bonds was very great. There were quoted reductions in values of 14 and 15 points before the former government went out of office. Interest rates declined following the summer of 1957 and they rose beginning in the summer of 1958. There was a rise until the autumn of 1959. After a period of stability they then began to decline again. This is the sort of thing that is going on in the markets of this continent. This also depends on the influence of the bond market in New York.
Now lest the impression be created in the minds of some hon. members that the government has brought about high interest rates let me point out that interest rates in this
Government Monetary Policy country, while they are higher than the government would like to see on borrowings that it has to make, are lower than the interest rates in the United Kingdom and have been close to the 1960 rates of interest in the United States, that country which is the largest reservoir of capital in the world and whose rates traditionally are lower than the interest rates in Canada. Let me just run quickly over some figures, Mr. Speaker, in respect of the 91-day treasury bill rates in Canada. Let us take the last three quarters of 1960 and compare them with the last three quarters of 1960 in respect of the United Kingdom.
And the United States.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
All right, I will read right across the page, and the figures will be in this order; Canada, U.S.A., and the U.K.
For the second quarter of 1960; Canada, 3.05; U.S.A., 3.09; U.K., 4.70. For the third quarter: Canada, 2.53; U.S.A., 2.39; U.K., 5.56. For the fourth quarter: Canada, 3.23; U.S.A., 2.36; U.K., 4.85. Those are treasury bill rates. The house is aware that treasury bill rates in Canada have declined since then.
Let us now take the quarterly averages of comparison of the long term interest rates, and again I will take just the last three quarters of 1960. Using the same order, the second quarter: Canada, 5.15; U.S.A., 4.11; U.K.,	5.41. For the third quarter:
Canada, 4.81; U.S.A., 3.82; U.K., 5.57. For the fourth quarter: Canada, 5.04; U.S.A., 3.90; U.K., 5.53.
Mr. Speaker, the Leader of the Opposition yesterday talked about the loss of confidence in the bond market. If confidence has not been lost in the value of government of Canada bonds it is not because the statements of the Leader of the Opposition have contributed anything to the confidence in this country. His effort in this respect has been destructive at all times, and I include what he said in respect of this subject yesterday. Surely the best test of whether there is confidence in the markets of Canada is to look at the figures of the public's holdings of Canada bonds. I could give the figures for some distance back but let me begin with those for 1959. I am giving these by quarters in respect of the general public holdings of government of Canada direct and guaranteed securities. For 1959, March 31, $9,499 million; June 30, $9,934 million; September 30, $10,132 million; December 31, $10,725 million. The same figures for 1960 beginning with March 31, $10,971 million; June 30, $10,800 million; September 30, $10,466 million; and December 31, $11,079 million, an all-time high. There

Government Monetary Policy is the answer to the Leader of the Opposition when he talks about loss of confidence in Canada bonds.
Let us look at the recent results. Even since December 20 when the supplementary budget sought to direct Canadians to do more of their borrowing in Canada, what has been the result? The fact is that provinces, municipalities and business have floated issues in the first six weeks of the year, or a little less, aggregating $200 million. The government of Canada put out an issue of $150 million, and none of this financing was done in New York. Has there been any disturbance in the interest rates in Canada in 1961, Mr. Speaker? No, there has not. The Canadian market has absorbed these issues and the market is even a little stronger today, and interest rates are a trifle lower than they were in the beginning of 1961, or on the date of the supplementary budget, being December 20, 1960.
After all this, the Leader of the Opposition yesterday expressed pious regret that the Bank of Canada has become, as he described it, the centre of the present controversy. Here are his words as found at page 2206 of Hansard:
It is most regrettable indeed that the Bank of Canada has become the centre of the present controversy-
Then he went on to say that it would weaken the prestige of an essential institution. I ask the Leader of the Opposition what he has done to prevent a weakening of the prestige of the Bank of Canada by bringing it into the centre of controversy? Is this any constructive contribution to understanding, fair play and fair judgement?
Then he had something to say on debt management. Debt management is an extremely important subject. It is a factor that is of importance to every person in Canada, no matter what may be his walk of life. This is clearly an area in which the government is responsible, as I have said on many occasions.
The Leader of the Opposition went on to charge that monetary policy has been subordinated in order to serve the interests of debt management. I do not believe that the Bank of Canada has subordinated monetary policy, which is its field, in order to serve the interests of debt management. As I have said, there has been no interference with monetary policy. Monetary policy can never operate in a modem country without regard to debt management policy. This government has applied definite, constructive and beneficial debt management policies. We certainly needed to do so because when we came into office we were bequeathed a doubtful legacy of debt with an extremely short term to it.


When we came into office the average term of Canada's debt was slightly over six years. Here are the figures. At June 30, 1957, in terms of general public holdings of direct and guaranteed securities, excluding Canada savings bonds and perpetuals, the average term to maturity was six years and eleven months; and in terms of government of Canada, direct and guaranted issues, excluding non-market issues and perpetuals, the average term to maturity of the outstanding holdings at June 30, 1957, was six years and two months. However, we went to work with a view to correcting this unsatisfactory situation which, under some circumstances, could even become dangerous. Our efforts to this end were made necessary as well as desirable by the condition which we inherited. When the Leader of the Opposition talks about timing, I think he had better go and examine in this respect his own nest that he bequeathed to us.
I do not think it would be profitable, Mr. Speaker, to go over the whole story again in reference to the conversion loan. I went into the history of the conversion loan at, I regret to say, considerable length in speaking in this house on April 28, 1959. My review of the conversion loan and the benefits which it brought begins at page 3113 of Hansard of that date and continues. Just to summarize it rather than to repeat, may I say that in that operation five outstanding victory loans that were overhanging the market and involving maturities that were going to begin the following year -the year after the conversion loan, in 1958-and aggregating $6,416,000,000, were the subject of the conversion loan. So great was the success of this most important and largest of all Canadian government financing operations that 90 per cent of those outstanding issues were converted and the result was a substantial contribution to stabilization of the bond market.
We completed this tremendous conversion undertaking none too soon because the market suffered on this continent a continued weakness running into the autumn and to the end of 1958; that weakness stemmed from New York. It was a great weakness in the New York market. Canada was not immune from it. Canada could not, in the nature of things, be immune from it. When the Leader of the Opposition attempts to attribute to the conversion loan the weakness that occurred in the markets on this continent in the autumn of 1958 his statement is fantastic nonsense. Is the Canadian government to be held responsible for a great weakness that developed in the New York bond market through the summer and particularly in the autumn of 1958?

When those crocodile tears course down his furrowed cheeks, Mr. Speaker, let us remember that everyone who converted his bonds not only obtained the advantage of a higher interest rate, the result of his own free decision in relation to conversion, but he also obtained the benefit of better market quotations on the new conversion bonds. Those bonds, with scarcely an exception at any subsequent time, were quoted at higher prices than were the victory loan bonds that were left outstanding in the hands of the owners.
The Leader of the Opposition, Mr. Speaker, has dredged up something that occurred three years ago, namely a great undertaking which he praised in generous terms in this house when it was announced in the summer of 1958. I was extremely grateful to him for the constructive statement he made on that occasion; it was a patriotic statement. It was just about the last constructive statement the Leader of the Opposition has made in this house.
That was before we knew how the minister was going to mess it up.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No. It was not
messed up. It was a great success.
The Leader of the Opposition yesterday talked about experts but he could not find any experts to quote. There are many experts in this field, people of acknowledged authority, who praised this operation and who in various countries expressed envy of the great and beneficial results of this enterprise in Canada.
How many has the minister quoted?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
When the Leader of the Opposition says as he did yesterday, that the conversion of the ninth victory loan cost hundreds of millions of dollars, he is talking plain nonsense. If any conversion loan was to be undertaken at all, it was absolutely essential that it should cover all five victory loan issues. It would not have been an adequate undertaking otherwise; it would have been a piecemeal undertaking. What is more, it would have not been equitable, efficient or economical. It would have been simply a piecemeal approach at very great cost to have simply converted the first two of those five victory loans. What is more, in the light of what happened in the bond market afterwards on this continent as a result of weakness in New York, Mr. Speaker, there would have been heavy increases in the interest costs to be met if we had not brought about that conversion and if we had allowed those victory loans to run to maturity and had then faced the problem of conversion. This was a
Government Monetary Policy farsighted and courageous attempt to meet the problem and it resulted in great benefits to Canada and in terms of debt management.
Let me set alongside those figures I gave earlier as to the average length of debt to maturity what was the situation after this conversion loan had been carried out. Whereas with respect to general public holdings at June 30, 1957, the average term was six years and eleven months, at September 30, 1958 it had risen to 14 years and nine months. In respect of outstanding government of Canada, direct and guaranteed securities, excluding non-market issues and perpetuals, the comparisons are as follows. At June 30, 1957, the average term to maturity was six years and two months; at September 30, 1958, it was ten years and six months. Is it any wonder that this great undertaking won praise in other countries which were envious of the tremendous improvement that had been brought about in our debt position in Canada?
The Leader of the Opposition, yesterday undertook to say something about the unemployment insurance fund, and he said some really weird things in this regard. He said in effect that when the conversion loan was undertaken, not only should the investment committee, operating under the Unemployment Insurance Act, not have converted but it should have turned everything into a virtually liquid position. Ninety-one day treasury bills; this was his theme. He said they should have looked far forward and seen that there would be heavy drains upon the unemployment insurance fund which would have to be met in cash.
It is too bad that these hon. gentlemen, when they were in office, did not have the prescience that they expect of others who follow them. The fact is that the illiquid position of the fund was not new. It merely reflected a continuation of the policy instituted several years earlier under the previous government.
But there was no drain on the fund.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
For the fund to obtain liquidity to the extent of one half of its holdings, as the Leader of the Opposition urged yesterday, would have required a forward view of continual high levels of unemployment which it would have been hard to justify in the summer of 1958 and would have involved the sacrifice of interest earnings on bonds that the unemployment insurance commission chose to hold and to acquire.
The fund did in fact convert the Canada victory loan bonds that it held, but it did not take the longest maturity of the new bond; it took the shortest maturity available

Government Monetary Policy to it. To suggest it should have sold all its victory bonds at the time of conversion surely implies support of the market by the Bank of Canada of the most massive kind.
The Leader of the Opposition apparently now thinks there should not have been a conversion. If there had not been any conversion and the fund had held its victory loan bonds, selling them when it needed, it would have suffered greater loss than indeed it did experience in selling its conversion bonds.
Not if they had sold them between July and October.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, should they have been able to look two years ahead and know exactly what was going to happen? If the hon. member for Essex East had been able to claim that kind of prescience I am quite sure he must have made a fortune at that time. If he could have seen what was going to happen two years ahead in the market he would have been the richest man in Canada today, as rich as Croesus.

Would the hon. minister permit a question? Does the minister agree that if the investment committee had permitted the sale of its securities between July and October, because the government guaranteed those bonds at par, at their full original value, they would not have lost as they did when they were forced into conversion?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It would have been a most improvident act by any proper standard for the unemployment insurance committee at that time to have sold out, without knowledge that would have needed the hindsight that the hon. member for Essex East enjoys so much today. It would have been improvident for it under the existing circumstances to have sold those bonds and denied itself the benefit of the higher interest yields that were available to it on the bonds. And in selling, it would have sent the market crashing.
You could not put holdings on the market for sale as massive as those of the unemployment insurance commission at that time without shaking the market to its foundations. That is the kind of policy, Mr. Speaker, that these authorities on the other side of the house are putting before us today as the one the unemployment insurance commission should have followed at that time. This is a most fatuous assertion and contention on the part of the official opposition.
The fact is that since October, 1958, the monthly average prices of victory loan bonds in the hands of the holders, those that remain, have been below those of the conversion bonds for all but seven months in this


whole period. The figure used yesterday by the Leader of the Opposition would assume that the fund would have liquidated back in 1958 not only its holdings of victory loan bonds but indeed all its holdings. He would in effect have asked the unemployment insurance commission to wreck the market by liquidation at that time of huge holdings that the bond market could not possibly absorb.
He would have destroyed the bond holdings of holders of Canada bonds to the extent of probably scores and scores of millions of dollars. That is what the Leader of the Opposition and the hon. member for Essex East say the unemployment insurance commission should have done; they say the unemployment insurance commission should have embarked on the liquidation of bond holdings running between $500 million and $1 billion at the time.
Can you imagine, Mr. Speaker, anything more utterly destructive to the bond market and to public confidence? The Canadian people will have reason to be thankful that the affairs of this country were not in those days, or since, in the hands of such utterly irresponsible people.
A $70 million dollar loss.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I would have thought-
The most serious violation of a trust fund in Canada's history, and you know it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: -the greatest mismanagement that could have occurred is the one suggested by the hon. member for Essex East in his utterly irresponsible way, when he concurred with the Leader of the Opposition who, if he does not know better himself, at least has advice available to him to guide him in these matters. I refer him to the former president of the Liberal association of Canada. He certainly would not have told him it would have been a responsible act for the unemployment insurance commission to attempt to liquidate between $500 million and $1 billion of Canada bonds that it held in 1958, throwing them on the market and wrecking the values of the bond holdings of other Canadians.
Why did you force them to sell?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Nothing could be more utterly shameful than a suggestion of that kind. How can anything be more utterly irresponsible than a proposal of that kind? I would think the hon. member for Essex East would want to hang his head after advocating anything as damaging and harmful to Canadian bonds as that.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Evidently you have not appreciated the utter folly of what was proposed yesterday by the hon. gentleman. Mr. Speaker, I had hoped to conclude my remarks long before this. I will say in this belated conclusion that we have had a most interesting kind of contradiction on the part of the official opposition.
Yesterday the Leader of the Opposition delivered what, having regard to the responsibilities, was quite clearly an attack on the governor of the Bank of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, on a point of order, the minister has no right to say that. I delivered no attack on the governor of the Bank of Canada. I delivered an attack on the government because of its irresponsible attitude in this matter. They abdicated their responsibility in this matter. I did not attack the governor of the Bank of Canada.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is not a point of order.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That, in the mind of the Leader of the Opposition, is supposed to be a point of order, a point of privilege. It is just an abuse of the rules of the house, Mr. Speaker, but the Leader of the Opposition-
You are an expert on that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: But I still feel toward the Leader of the Opposition the respect that a former student owes to his professor,-
I thought that would come in.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
-a respect which lingers. I recall what a good lecturer he was in history, even though economics never came within the scope of his learning.
I do not say this was a personal attack on the governor of the bank, but it was an attack upon the policy of the bank, upon the policy followed by the governor of the bank-
It was not.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: -because the policy he was condemning and criticizing so strongly yesterday is the policy of the bank and of the governor of the bank.
You accept the policy.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I put that alongside what was said in this house by his deskmate, the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) on December 8 last as reported at page 609 of Hansard. The hon. member for Laurier rose to ask me a question in these words:
May I direct a question to the Minister of Finance, and ask whether in view of the statement
Government Monetary Policy made by several economists of Canadian universities concerning the governor of the Bank of Canada, as headlined in this morning's press, the minister proposes to make a statement expressing confidence in the management of the bank.
The hon. member for Laurier thought the management of the bank was entitled to an expression of confidence. The Leader of the Opposition yesterday attacked hip and thigh the policy of the Bank of Canada, which is the governor's sole responsibility. So I say that here we have two deskmates-
Don't crawl out from under.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
-who are apparently completely at loggerheads. It is a great pity that they cannot get their heads together.
Now we have before us an amendment by the official opposition which attempts to put on the record of parliament something which is a denial of the facts. It attempts to say that the government of Canada, regardless of the fact that parliament has legislated otherwise, is responsible for monetary policy in Canada. It has been the decision of parliament from the outset, when this bank was set up, that monetary policy should be the responsibility of the Bank of Canada and that the government cannot interfere in the bank's management of monetary policy. Therefore, this Liberal amendment invites parliament to contradict itself, and I am sure the House of Commons has no intention of doing so.
I think the subamendment introduced this afternoon by the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) merits only one very brief comment. It asks the house to add to this contradictory thesis expressed in the Liberal amendment a further expression of regret that the lack of constructive government planning with regard to monetary and debt policies has resulted in the deepening of the unemployment crisis. It has not resulted in any deepening of the unemployment crisis. The government has followed a consistent and proper course in this matter. It has recognized that parliament has already legislated in this matter of responsibility concerning the management of monetary policy. This government does not place itself above parliament. It recognizes its responsibility to parliament. This kind of amendment could emanate only from those who still retain the imprint of that government which went out of office in June 1957, because it had lost all sense of responsibility to the sovereign House of Commons.

The
house has just listened for almost two hours to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) dealing with the amendment to his supply motion, an amendment which reads, in part:

Government Monetary Policy The house regrets the refusal of the government to accept and discharge its proper responsibility in the field of monetary policy and its demonstrable incompetence to manage the public debt in the interests of the Canadian people.
If any proof were needed of the timeliness and validity of this amendment it is to be found in the speech which the Minister of Finance has made this afternoon. The hon. gentleman chose for 20 minutes of the time taken by him to avoid discussing the subject altogether and to point out that the opposition should have chosen another subject for discussion. Throughout the rest of the time allocated to him-and the hon. gentleman has no time limit to observe, while the rest of us are left with a limitation which is somewhat severe at times-

Your
limitations are not only those of time.

I appreciate the bright
remarks of the Postmaster General but I am sure the subject is of no interest to him. Perhaps he could allow those who are concerned about it to debate it. Hon. members on the other side may differ from my conclusions, and others may agree with them, but I am entitled to make them and, surely, the Postmaster General could discharge his duty as a minister of the crown in a better manner than by making remarks and interjections of that kind.
The point I was making is that even if there were no confusion in the public mind about the government's responsibility in the field of monetary policy in the past, there is now because of the hon. gentleman's pronouncements this afternoon. I take it to be implicit in the minister's speech that the government does have a responsibility for fiscal policy. I think that is common ground between us. I take it, also, that the hon. gentleman admits that the government has responsibility in the field of debt management. That, also, is common ground. I take it that it is only when we get to the area of monetary policy that we differ. The minister says that has been given to the Bank of Canada, and that the government no longer has responsibility over it. It is on that point that we differ, and differ very sharply.
Who has responsibility, then?

The government did, and the government still has responsibility over monetary policy. It is unthinkable that any government of any sovereign nation should not have responsibility for monetary policy and it was never suggested otherwise until the present minister was made Minister of Finance. Then he changed his views on the matter and advanced the theory he outlined this afternoon. In the few minutes I have

left to me in which to deal with this question I intend	to	quote briefly	what	some	ofour ministers	of	finance have	had to say	onthe subject. In 1936, Mr. Dunning, dealing with the Bank of Canada legislation, had this to say	as	reported on	page	3262	of
Hansard of that year:
The bank may and should resist temporary gusts of public fancy, but in the long run it must show responsiveness	to	public opinion. In	the long
run, the bank in the performance of a vital sovereign function must be responsible to the sovereign will expressed through government. There cannot be two sovereigns in a single state.
That was the position taken in the debate in 1936. Then we come to the discussion of this subject in 1941. Mr. Ilsley, on June 13 of that year, had something to say on the subject and I quote him from page 3936 from the Hansard of that date. I should like to quote at greater length but hon. members will forgive me if I quote only parts of what was said. I will give the page reference in each case so that members can read further if they wish. On June 13, 1941 Mr. Ilsley said:
The point which I would like to emphasize is that the responsibility with which the governor and board have been charged by parliament does not in any way relieve the government of responsibility for the monetary policy being pursued by the bank, nor in any way militate against public control of monetary policy. The monetary policy which the bank carries out from time to time must be the government's monetary policy, but the government must leave the carrying out of that policy-
Note that-"the carrying out of that policy".
*-the choice of ways and means of executing it, to the management of the bank in whose judgment it has confidence.
If the government is satisfied with the policy which is being pursued, there is obviously no quarrel between it and the bank. Let us suppose, however, that the management of the bank and the government do not see eye to eye in the matter of monetary policy. Let us assume that after the usual careful consideration of the pros and cons, a serious difference of opinion remains. In such a case there can be no question whatever as to the outcome of the dispute. The government's views will prevail.
Here it is. That is the difference. That is responsibility.

The views of Mr. Abbott will be found on page 4393 of Hansard of June 20, 1951. After a question had been pressed upon him, Mr. Abbott replied:
The government, of course, if it were not satisfied with the action taken by the governor and the directors of the Bank of Canada, would have to change the management of the bank.
After an interjection of the word "yes" by Mr. Low, Mr. Abbott concluded:
So that I suppose it is fair to assume that the ultimate responsibility must fall upon the government.

The minister referred to the questioning of the then governor of the Bank of Canada, Mr. Graham Towers, in the banking and commerce committee in 1954. I refer hon. gentlemen to pages 714 and 715 of the unrevised committee reports of March 18, 1954. On that occasion the governor of the bank dealt with this subject. Hon. gentlemen will recall that the minister quoted part of this and that I asked the minister a question about it. He had stopped at a certain point in the quotation and I asked him to read the subsequent lines. The portion of the statement I requested the minister to read is as follows:
On the other hand, there is no alibi possible for the government, because if government said, well, we disagreed with what the central bank did, but parliament has placed the responsibility on them, so what could we do? The answer obviously is that the administration of the day, supported by a majority in parliament, can always alter the legislation. In fact, I doubt whether a disagreement would ever necessitate such a thing, because there are various ways and means by which directors and management can be got rid of. I am sure that in the case of a serious disagreement that is what would take place.
Mr. Towers then went on to elaborate on that subject. Under examination by the present Minister of Finance, who was then the private hon. member for Eglinton and a member of the official opposition, Mr. Towers made it perfectly clear that the government had the ultimate responsibility and that if there were a disagreement, the governor of the Bank of Canada would have to resign. That is perfectly clear.
He has changed his mind now.
The minister then made reference on this point to a statement made by Mr. Harris, I believe on June 10, 1956.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: August.

The minister quoted from Hansard of that date. I wish to point out one or two features of the question and answer period on the orders of the day of August 10, 1956 to which the minister made reference earlier. One feature is that Mr. Harris made it very clear that he was advised of the action-taken. The then prime minister went on to make it clear that the government of the day had complete confidence in what was done. The government was in accord with it. There was no confusion about a possible difference of view.
I am not certain if the Minister of Finance quoted the following statement made by the then prime minister as found at page 7352 of Hansard of August 10, 1956 in answer to one of the many questions that arose on that occasion:
-I can assure the hon. gentleman that the matter received very serious consideration and the government has not decided to recommend
Government Monetary Policy
to parliament any amendment to the act which places that responsibility on the governor of the Bank of Canada.
It was made clear in that question and answer period that the issue that was being dealt with was that the action should be taken through the Bank of Canada. I do not think anyone has contested that. I have re-read that debate very carefully today. As I read it there was no suggestion that the government could abdicate its responsibility in the field.
It is interesting that at the conclusion of the question and answer period-and I remember the occasion well because there was some heat generated in that period-
Mr. Speaker, would the hon. member permit a question?
No. I have only 17 minutes left. If the hon. member would like to direct his question to me when I conclude my remarks I will be happy to deal with it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: That is a good way of not dealing with it.

I am really perfectly happy to accept the hon. member's question but I have only 17 minutes left at my disposal. In that time I want to develop my argument as best I can. I will be quite happy to deal with questions at the conclusion of my remarks.
I was about to point out that at the conclusion of the question and answer period the request was made that the then minister of finance deal with this subject on his estimates next day. The next day, on his estimates, the minister did deal with the subject at some length. He made it abundantly clear that the government did have the responsibility, and spoke also of the government's agreement with the decision taken by the bank. The references to this matter will be found mainly at page 7457 of Hansard of August 11, 1956. Let me place on the record a statement made by Mr. Harris on that occasion:
The government is satisfied, and I believe that the vast majority of informed observers are satisfied, that under the economic conditions of the past 12 months it was desirable to moderate the rate of monetary expansion. I know of no responsible person who argues openly for inflation as a solution to the problem of excess demand.
Further along Mr. Harris said:
It is right and proper that our fiscal system at this juncture should emphasize additional restraint in public spending wherever possible. It is equally appropriate that monetary policy should assist by exerting a moderating influence on the expansion of credit.
That is taking responsibility.

He did not shirk his responsibility.

Government Monetary Policy

No, there was no question of his shirking responsibility. If hon. members will read the evidence given in the banking and commerce committee of 1954, they will find that there was no suggestion made then by the then private hon. member for Eglinton who is now Minister of Finance of the government shirking responsibility.
Or by the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell).
Yes. Indeed, the hon. member for Greenwood was most eloquent about the sovereignty of parliament at that time.
The hon. gentleman certainly was.

This subject has always been treated in that way up until the time the present government took office. The situation is different now. The Minister of Finance seems to seek to say today that this is all the responsibility of the Bank of Canada. Notwithstanding his physical vigour in speaking and his pugnacious qualities, the minister attempts to depict himself as a poor little help'ess man. The Minister of Finance has nothing to say about this policy and could not have any part in it, poor little creature. This is the Minister of Finance who displays great physical vigour in argument, perhaps in an attempt to conceal the lack of careful reasoning that should be applied to a subject of this kind.
The minister in support of his argument chose to quote from the Bank of Canada Act and I should like to place on the record some of its references to the governor in council.
Mr. Speaker, may I call it six o'clock.
At six o'clock the house took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The house resumed at 8 p.m.

Mr. Speaker, when the house rose for the dinner adjournment at six o'clock I had started to make reference to the treatment of the legislation, the Bank of Canada Act, by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming). We had the extraordinary spectacle of the Minister of Finance on this subject making no reference at all to the request of the opposition that the whole matter of the operations of the Bank of Canada be referred to the committee on banking and commerce. Instead he took the position that the government had no responsibility whatever in the field of monetary policy and said, that the subject matter of monetary policy belonged exclusively to the Bank of Canada.
[Mr. Martin (Essex East).!

The minister made some references to the Bank of Canada Act. In the few moments at my disposal I propose to show some of the authority left in the governor in council or the Minister of Finance, as the case may be, under the Bank of Canada Act and to show that the Minister of Finance was not, as he pictured himself this afternoon, bereft of all authority over the Bank of Canada.
The first section I should like to refer to is section 4(2) under which branches and agencies of the bank can only be established with the authority of the governor in council. Under section 5(2) the deputy minister of finance is made a member of the board of directors. He does not have the right to vote but either the deputy minister of finance or such other officer as the minister may designate is made a member of the board. Obviously that is for the purpose of keeping the minister fully informed. Under section 6(1) the governor and deputy governor can only be appointed with the approval of the governor in council. In section 6(3)(a) provision is made for tenure of office of the governor and deputy governor and under paragraph (c) the remuneration of the governor and deputy governor can only be set with the approval of the governor in council.
Under section 9 the minister appoints the directors for terms of three years, so he has exclusive control over that. The removal of directors because of incapacity can only be done with the approval of the governor in council. Then there is a very important provision in section 14. The governor of the bank may veto any action of the board of directors or of the executive committee and if such veto power is exercised the veto must be submitted to the Minister of Finance and the governor in council may confirm or disallow the veto. That is an absolute and very wide power over any action taken by the governor in that connection.
There are other such provisions. Section 17(1) provides that the amount of the capital of the bank is controlled by the governor in council. Section 17(2) provides how the capital shall be divided into shares and that all the shares will be issued to the minister. He is the only shareholder. Under section 20, subsection 2, the bank, when required by the Minister of Finance to do so, shall act as the agent of the government in certain respects concerning the management of the public debt of Canada.
The minister made a lot of section 21(1) which reads as follows:
The bank has the sole right to issue notes payable to bearer on demand and intended for circulation in Canada-
And so on. He argued that that had something to do with his authority vis-a-vis that

of the bank. It is nothing of the sort. When the bank legislation was first enacted each chartered bank could issue its own notes and this provision took away the right of the chartered banks to issue their own notes and gave it to the central bank. The conclusion drawn by the minister from that provision is not an accurate one at all. As a matter of fact, the section goes on to give the governor in council control over the denominations of these notes. The minister's argument on that point is quite specious.
Under section 22(2) the governor in council has certain authority over suspension of the bank to sell gold. In section 23(3) the governor in council is given the power to suspend the gold reserve requirement. In a couple of places in section 24 the receiver general has certain authority over the rest fund, the receiver general, of course, being the Minister of Finance. Section 25(1) gives the governor in council the right to appoint auditors. Section 25(4) gives the minister the right to require the auditors to report to him from time to time. Section 26(1) deals with weekly statements of assets and liabilities. The minister can require such statements and he can prescribe the form. Under section 26(2) a weekly statement of notes is required. Section 26(3) provides for monthly statements of assets and liabilities. Section 26(5) gives power to the governor in council to amend any of the schedules.
Under section 27(2) the governor in council or the minister may require certain other statements. Section 27(2) has to do with the annual report and statements of that type. Section 33(1) deals with the bylaws of the bank and they can only be enacted with the approval of the governor in council.
In other words, the minister struggled very hard to show that the act gives all the powers to the Bank of Canada and leaves him as minister-a man of such energy-bereft of any power in this field. As I have shown by these references to the legislation, the act does nothing of the sort.
The minister also made some references to the conversion loan. Let me tell him that the conversion loan was a monument to his failure in the field of debt management. He should never have included the seventh, eighth and ninth victory loans in the conversion loan and because of his doing so there was incurred some $330 million by way of added interest and carrying charges, as well as a great many other adverse effects. Because he included them in his conversion loan it was necessary for him to make his debt management policies override all other policies and encroach on them in a way that was never imagined before.
Government Monetary Policy
One of the fields where monetary policy was subjected to his debt management policy because of his wrong handling of the conversion loan by including all these victory loans was the unemployment insurance fund. This afternoon the minister gave figures and a picture that were quite misleading to the house. I do not say he did so intentionally but he put an interpretation on the position taken by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) that was wholly wrong. The Leader of the Opposition never for one moment suggested that the conversion loan bonds should all be dumped on the market at one time and depress the market. What happened there was that some half of the assets of the unemployment insurance fund at the time of the conversion were victory loans. Of that figure some $90 million were due within two years; that is, they would have matured within a two-year period and have been paid off at par. Of course, if at the time of conversion the victory loans had not been included in the conversion loan their maturities would have met the fund requirements and their value would have held up. I want to point out that the minister in that action made the management of the fund subservient to his debt management requirements, having all public funds converted rather than fulfilling his duty as trustee of this fund, which is provided by employees, employers and taxpayers of Canada. This accounted for the loss, as will be seen from an answer appearing in Hansard of February 15, and from a sessional paper tabled December 21, 1960. This loss by reason of converting the bonds amounted to something in the neighbourhood of $70 million. That misuse of his duties in the field of debt management overrode his duty as trustee. The minister's responsibility as trustee of the fund became subservient to the minister's responsibility in respect of debt management policies of this government. Had he been in a private field outside the government, this wrong action would have left him liable for the loss resulting therefrom. This untenable action-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: It was certainly not untenable.
It is untenable, that is a true statement.

The minister is trying to make the house believe that he has no authority and no responsibility in the field of monetary policy. He says that parliament can deal with these things. Under our constitutional procedure when parliament has responsibility-I do not subscribe to his view of it at all-surely it is the responsibility of the government and the minister concerned

Division
to bring forward the legislation. The minister was so timorous in that field that he did not tell us anything about any responsibility that he does have in this field. He also did not tell us, having taken the position that he is not responsible, although he is the minister of the crown with the responsibility in the field of finance, whether he agrees or disagrees with the monetary policy in Canada that has been carried out since August, 1957-

speechtext:
Order. I am sorry to interrupt the hon. member. It being 8.15 o'clock it is my duty pursuant to section 4 (d) of standing order 56 to put forthwith the question on any amendments now before the house.
