maintopic: COAL-REQUEST FOR ACTION ON CLOSING OF MINES
COAL-REQUEST FOR ACTION ON CLOSING OF MINES
speechtext:
On
March 3, 1959 I introduced in this house a grievance based on the failure of the government to take adequate action to meet the demands of the coal industry. On that occasion I pointed out the seriousness of the coal situation which, since this government took office in June 1957, has reached the proportions of a major crisis calling for immediate action and appropriate measures of adjustment to cope with an urgent situation.
My reason for rising this evening is strengthened by the inability of the government to meet its pre-election commitments and its persistent failure to solve the problems of the coal industry. In the course of my remarks I intend to call attention to the inconsistency of the government's actions, its failure to appreciate the seriousness of the situation and its lack of understanding of a serious problem which must be met face on and handled with a bold and comprehensive determination to undertake a social adjustment in a depressed area where a segment of our population is menaced with grave financial distress and a most insecure future.
As long ago as June 30, 1958, I introduced in this house a motion condemning the government for backing away from its commitment to promote and develop the industry in the Atlantic provinces, and especially for its failure to prevent or avert shutdowns in the Nova Scotia mines. Reference was made to my motion by the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan) and on page 1800 of Hansard for July 1, 1958 the hon. gentleman said of it:
This is one of the great motions of want of confidence in the House of Commons, one of the six motions to go into supply when the substantial omissions of the government are brought to the attention of the house. If this is all the opposition could arraign this government on, then certainly the record of the government is very good indeed.
These were the words of the Minister of National Revenue when we sought to direct the attention of the government to a situation which, we believed, was heading for a major crisis. That crisis exists today. When we in the opposition were urging the government to act without delay to solve a problem affecting an important segment of the population of the maritime provinces we were told that

Coal Industry
we were attacking a matter which was of minor importance. We were told that we were paying attention to a subject which, in the minister's view, was of very little significance-hardly worth while as the subject matter of a grievance raised on a supply motion.
On that particular occasion we were told by the Minister of National Revenue that the stockpile of coal was roughly 1,400,000 tons but that there were orders for 4,600,000 tons and that orders were still coming in. Here are the minister's own words as reported at page 1801 of Hansard for July 1, 1958:
It is going to take months, perhaps into the winter, perhaps even into next spring before the whole stockpile is liquidated: and liquidated it will be, because the company will see to it that it moves out and, as I have said, the orders are recurring and multiplying.
And further on the minister went as far as to say, and I quote again his own words which will be found on page 1804 of Hansard for the same date:
The government believe that the future of the Nova Scotia coal industry can be re-established and is reasonably bright. We have seen an example within the last few days, when the Ontario hydro commission chairman said that within a year or two he would be buying well over one million tons of coal and that within 10 years, even after making allowances for the St. Lawrence seaway and all the other developments of hydroelectric power-he, or rather the hydro commission, would be buying over 10 million tons of coal according to the present expansion program for Ontario.
What is the situation today? Where is that
4,600,000	ton order? Where is that one million ton order for Ontario, referred to by the minister in July, 1958, almost three years ago? Where are all these orders which were recurring and multiplying?
The Toronto Globe and Mail for December 7, 1960 reports as follows:
Hydro denies coal commitment.
The Ontario Hydro-Electric Power Commission must buy its coal at competitive prices and has made no commitment to purchase Nova Scotia coal, a commission spokesman said last night.
I know that government speakers will outline with some personal satisfaction what they have done since taking office to assist the coal industry. I know that in July of 1958 the government took some temporary measures, such as extending the existing subventions in order to prevent more extensive layoffs in the industry.
The fact remains, however, that the government has failed to introduce adequate measures and has shown that it was not capable of grappling with a problem of this magnitude. The present government has been dragging its feet. It has failed to come up with a well thought out program; it has failed once

more to recognize the seriousness and importance of a situation affecting 8,000 to
10.000	miners and a population of close to
150.000	people.

Mr. Speaker, I have extensive notes and extensive quotations and I am following those quotations word for word.
On June 30, 1958 I warned the government of the seriousness of the situation. On page 1757 of Hansard of that date I am reported as having said:
The present government's policy gives no assurance whatsoever to the coal mines of the Atlantic provinces that at the end of the present year the excess carryover and stockpile accumulated will not force a further lay-off which could be much more serious than the shutdown now taking place.
That is exactly what is happening today. We were accused of being prophets of gloom and doom, of exaggerating the situation. Eight months later, on March 3, 1959, I reminded the government of its failure to meet the demands of the coal industry. I brought to the attention of this house the meeting which was held on February 2 with the Prime Minister and other federal ministers and a delegation from Nova Scotia headed by Premier Stanfield. On that occasion the premier urged increased subventions on an emergency basis as the best means of staving off further lay-offs.
I warned the government that subventions and subventions alone would not keep the miners of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick at work, and would not prevent some of the mining towns of Nova Scotia from becoming ghost towns. I offered suggestions then-concrete suggestions-which at the time were sneered at by representatives on the government side of this house, of areas which are directly affected by the decision recently arrived at concerning certain mines in the Cape Breton area.
The very same hon. member of this house who said on March 3, 1959 as reported at page 1575 of Hansard of that date that my solution meant "fewer miners, less production, no surplus"; the same hon. member who said that my suggestion meant "train fare out of the country" for displaced miners, that very same hon. member is now urging the government to take action on the suggestion which I made in this house two years ago. That hon. gentleman is asking the government to intervene with the Avro company, and Dosco

in an effort to persuade them to establish in Cape Breton and not near Montreal their proposed steel rolling plant.
I wish now to refer to an article which appeared in the Halifax Chronicle-Herald. of February 20, 1961 under the headline, "Cape Breton MP's Call for Immediate 'Crash Program' The article reads, in part:
An eight-point program to stimulate Cape Breton's economy involving increased expenditure in five government departments and a new conference with Dominion Coal Company aimed at averting or delaying the shutdown of three major coal mines was placed before Prime Minister Diefen-baker Sunday.
Instead of supporting our concrete suggestions in this house, hon. members opposite prefer sundry meetings with the Prime Minister.
Here is what I had to say about this project, not in 1961-not when it is too late-but two years ago on March 3, 1959 as reported at page 1574 of Hansard:
The Avro company should have been influenced to establish in Cape Breton and not near Montreal their proposed steel rolling plant. The government should have intervened and provided the company with every argument and if need be even financial assistance in order to influence it to open this new mill in the Atlantic provinces in the vicinity of the coal mining area.
Instead of sneering at my remarks, hon. members opposite, and particularly those from the areas affected should have used their good influence with the government for the realization of this project, when it was still not too late to intervene.
Hon. members opposite must admit, in view of recent events in the coal industry, that action should be taken at once, even if it means substantial tax concessions or other forms of assistance to provide new industries, preferably with coal as their basis, which would at least restore the economy of the industry to its 1957 level and alleviate this atmosphere of uncertainty and insecurity, this fear and gloom which prevails in Cape Breton today.

maintopic: COAL-REQUEST FOR ACTION ON CLOSING OF MINES

maintopic: COAL-REQUEST FOR ACTION ON CLOSING OF MINES

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
maintopic: COAL-REQUEST FOR ACTION ON CLOSING OF MINES
speechtext: Order.

maintopic: COAL-REQUEST FOR ACTION ON CLOSING OF MINES
speechtext:
I say that if 2,000 or 3,000 miners have to be retired from the mines, they must be provided with work at industrial plants located at the pitheads and only then will the problem be solved for years to come.
If two years ago those hon. members who are today urging the government to take action had used their good influence to have this steel rolling plant located in the Sydney
Coal Industry
area it would have taken care of at least
1,000	of these miners. Will the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker), will the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan), will the silent Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys (Mr. Comtois) once more attempt to convince the population of Cape Breton that they have been deeply concerned with their problems? Will the Prime Minister convince the population of Cape Breton that, as he stated in the house on June 27, 1958, as found on page 1689 of Hansard, "every sympathetic consideration will be given to assure the bringing about of a state of affairs which will ameliorate to the maximum degree possible this very trying and serious problem"?
The present government, Mr. Speaker, in its election promises in 1957 and again in 1958 gave great hopes, great expectations to the coal mining population of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. The fact remains, however, that on August 20, 1959, 14 months after we had introduced our supply motion in the house, the Prime Minister announced the appointment of a royal commission on coal. In making the announcement the Prime Minister said that the government felt that the coal problem was a special one and so urgent as to require a special inquiry rather than to be considered by the Borden commission on energy. The Prime Minister admitted at the time, over a year and a half ago, that, and I quote his own words, "subsidies alone were not a final answer to the coal problem", and he indicated that a thorough study of the long term market outlook was required. There again the Prime Minister admitted that a readjustment of coal production had to be made in such a way that the industry would serve its future markets efficiently and economically.
The coal problem was an urgent one when we introduced our motion on June 30, 1958. The coal problem was critical when the Prime Minister announced the appointment of the Rand commission on August 20, 1959. The coal situation had deteriorated further when the report of the Rand commission was made public late in September of last year.
The report of the Rand commission, Mr. Speaker, has now been in the hands of the government for over five months. For months Dosco had made it clear that three mines employing 2,600 men will definitely close this year. The dates have now been fixed at May 31, July 1 and August 12 respectively. For months the government has been aware that the Caledonia mine, the Florence and No. 16 will be closed during 1961.
What has been done to take care of this emergency? On November 23 the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys saw fit to give

Coal Industry
the house a statement concerning the implementation of the report of the royal commission on coal. What did he have to say on that occasion? Here are the minister's own words as recorded on page 111 of Hansard:
In short, the Rand report is the type of public document which demands the most serious study from each of us.
I agree with him on that.
It is also the type of document which demands the most serious, systematic and meticulous study by the government. I can inform you that such a study by the government is in progress. It is occupying the attention of an interdepartmental committee consisting of senior officers of the Department of Finance, the Department of Trade and Commerce, the Department of Labour, the privy council office, the national energy board and the dominion coal board, under the chairmanship of a senior officer of mines and technical surveys.
The committee has been given clear and specific instructions. It is "to study and report to the cabinet on the recommendations of the royal commission on coal relating to subsidies and research" and on such representations as have been received by the government.
I hope, Mr. Speaker, that the minister has in mind making public the Vissac report which we have been asking the government to table for over a week. Those were the words of the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys. The Rand report had been in the hands of the government for two months, and once again we have a government unable to take a decision, a government seeking more delaying tactics before making up its mind. It was a delaying tactic, as I said a while ago, when the commission was appointed on August 20, 1959. It was again a delaying tactic when an interdepartmental committee was appointed in the fall of 1960.
What has the government been doing in the meantime to protect the coal industry? As was so well said in a recent editorial in the Casket of Antigonish on February 9:
The mood of the average Nova Scotian at the moment is one of lack of faith in the power of the federal government either to recognize fully the problems which face us or to tackle the problems with the required vigour. We feel that Ottawa is either not interested in the problems of a province which, after all, has only 12 seats in a 265-seat House of Commons, or that it is simply not capable of grappling with a problem of this magnitude. In either case, Nova Scotians have every right indeed to be very disappointed with the lack of action at Ottawa.
What has the government done since the appointment of the interdepartmental committee to study the recommendations of the Rand report? On January 9, in an attempt to distract attention from another important event which was taking place in Ottawa on that day, the Minister of National Revenue and the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys issued a joint statement to the press. Their statement said that Caledonia No. 4 in
Glace Bay, due to close January 14, would be kept alive until May 31 and that the Florence mine and No. 16 at New Waterford would continue operations until July 1 and August 12 of this year respectively.
In other words, the government has officially announced that it is prepared to accept the closure of three mines in the Cape Breton area; that it is prepared to accept the laying off of close to 3,000 coal miners, thus wiping out the means of livelihood of tens of thousands of our population. This action of the government has made a farce of the Rand report. It has made a farce of the interdepartmental committee appointed last fall to study this report. The government has repudiated that part of the Rand report on page 30 which stated:
We cannot cut this island off, and Canada acting with Nova Scotia must, in my opinion, provide conditions to enable it to regain confidence and affirm its will to a new vitality.
The government by this action has repudiated that part of the Rand report on page 42 which stated:
The need exists in Cape Breton to build up alternative means of productive wealth; and the necessity also of facing up to such a possibility as well as the planning for the minimum disruption in the substitution. It is to try to avoid severe dislocation even within ten years that the recommendations provide for graduated action.
The position of the present government on this matter of vital importance is ambiguous. It is one of delayed action, one of uncertainty and insecurity for the miners and the population generally. The government is acting with regard to this problem in the same uncertain and inactive way it dealt with the Arrow, with Elliot Lake, with Springhill. What has it done for the displaced miners of Springhill, for this unfortunate community which through no fault of its residents was almost overnight forced by a tragedy into the state of a ghost town? It is not a prison farm, it is not $10,000 in winter works, to which the federal government will contribute about $3,000 and which will employ about 14 men for a few days, that will take care of the displaced miners of Springhill. The present government, I repeat, is dragging its feet. It is shirking its responsibility. It is refusing to take adequate measures to solve the coal problems of the maritimes. It has agreed to accept the closure of at least three mines without making any move to find alternate jobs for the miners who will be laid off by such closures. It has agreed to accept closures of three mines when an interdepartmental committee of its own appointment was studying the recommendations of a royal commission. What are we to expect next? Probably an announcement by the Prime Minister or a joint statement by the

Minister of National Revenue and the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys to the effect that the government has decided to appoint a royal commission to study the report of the interdepartmental committee on its study of the report of the Rand commission.
I repeat, Mr. Speaker, this government has made a farce of the interdepartmental committee appointed to study the Rand report. This government is refusing to take an overall approach to the whole problem of the coal producing areas. The postponement for a few months of the closing of the three mines in Cape Breton is by no means a permanent solution to these problems. This government has failed to introduce plans for the situation that will arise when apparently the mines must be closed. No steps whatsoever have been taken to relocate the displaced miners, no plans are being made for the future. This is typical of the day-to-day attitude of this government.
The coal industry of Cape Breton will not subsist on subsidies and on subsidies alone. Instead of its sit back and wait attitude, this government must wake up from its lethargy and face the facts. This government must agree to contribute a substantial sum for capital projects in the Atlantic area to be spread over a relatively short period of years.
As I have said before in this house, the government by transferring the coal problem to a committee of civil servants is shrinking away from its responsibility; it is announcing postponement after postponement in dealing with the urgent problem of the coal industry. The government has asked Mr. Rand to make recommendations. Mr. Rand presented his recommendations. Now the government is asking another committee to make recommendations on what it should do with the Rand recommendations. Why is the government stalling; why is it dragging its feet? Is it because there is division; there is disunity among cabinet ministers on this vital problem? I know that some of the recommendations of the Rand report, if implemented, would be detrimental to the coal industry in New Brunswick. The spread in the subsidy payments between Nova Scotia and New Brunswick is too apparent for any government to act according to that particular aspect of the recommendations. The Minister of Forestry (Mr. Flemming), during his by-election campaign last fall, committed himself in no uncertain terms as to the position he would take on the Rand report recommendations. Is this sufficient reason, however, for the government, for the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys, to refuse to state their attitude, their policy on the coal situation?
As I have already said, in my view the recommendations in the report do not provide
Coal Industry
a satisfactory answer to the human and social problems that are involved in the cut-backs and now in the contemplated closures in the Cape Breton coal fields, nor to the requirement of the coal industry in the province of New Brunswick. Once again I want to put forward a number of suggestions which in my mind the government ought to consider, and consider now, in relation to the urgent problem of the Cape Breton coal area. First, if the government accepts the views of Commissioner Rand that mine closures must take place within the foreseeable future-and this the government has already accepted according to the joint statement from the Minister of National Revenue and the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys which I have referred to earlier-then I maintain that these closures cannot be permitted to occur abruptly and suddenly, because no prior planning has yet been made. The government was warned about this almost three years ago but to date it has refused to act.
As the government has now accepted the view that closures are inevitable, such closures should be allowed to occur only gradually and over a period of time during which, if necessary, the government should underwrite losses of the company to the break-even point. This interim period would provide an opportunity for further planning and investigation as to what can be done to meet the unemployment problem that would surely follow closures. This would give the government the opportunity to do now what it should have done three years ago.
Second, I believe that the government should direct the dominion coal board to explore with the company the economies of a new development at the Lingan area of Cape Breton and, especially, whether federal assistance in opening a new mine might be justified in the long run through substantial reduction in production costs that would make coal more competitive as a source of energy.

The member who has just taken his seat has referred to his knowledge of the coal industry. If there is anyone in the house that doubts his statement just ask the member from Gloucester (Mr. Robi-haud), because not too long ago he arrived in the town of Glace Bay and advertised himself in the Cape Breton Post as the official coal critic for the official opposition. Later that same day, while visiting one of the mines in that area, in a discussion with the newspaper people who were covering his visit he candidly admitted that this was his first visit to a coal mine of that type. Following that admission he expressed no surprise at the cost of production. Here we have a

man who claims knowledge of the coal industry, and who arrives in a coal mining town advertising himself as the official critic for the official opposition in respect of coal, and then admits that it was his first visit to a coal mine.
The hon. member has taken it upon himself to read many quotations. In fact, his speech was made up mostly of quotations from what somebody else had said about coal in the past. He went so far as to give the members from Cape Breton a pat on the back for what they had been trying to do and I thank him for that gesture. But I would remind him that, while he was on his feet, at no time did he take any exception to the fact that New Brunswick is about to burn oil in the thermal plant. He did not take his government to task for that fact. The miners in New Brunswick are riding on the backs of the Cape Breton miners who came up here to Ottawa to make representations on behalf of the Cape Breton coal miners. The miners of New Brunswick had every advantage of it. The miners of Cape Breton, through their representation, are helping to carry on the coal industry in New Brunswick. Further than that, Mr. Speaker-

maintopic: COAL-REQUEST FOR ACTION ON CLOSING OF MINES

maintopic: COAL-REQUEST FOR ACTION ON CLOSING OF MINES

maintopic: COAL-REQUEST FOR ACTION ON CLOSING OF MINES

I will consider it to be a question of privilege for the benefit of the hon. member. He has yet to attend any coal conference since this government came into office. I have never missed one, and I have never seen him in attendance. If he wishes to do so, he can take that as a question of privilege. I will not withdraw my statement, because I will not withdraw from the truth.
He has made reference to what has gone on in the coal industry. From 1946 to 1956 34 coal mines closed in Nova Scotia. I should like to see where on the record he has raised any objection about his administration. Let me tell you something else about

his administration, Mr. Speaker. The former prime minister went into his own province and told the people of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick to leave the coal in the ground for the benefit of future generations for the manufacture of synthetic articles. He said that in New Brunswick. I do not care what was said by the hon. member who represents Bonavista-Twillingate. I said "represents"; he does not come from Bonavista-Twillingate. I do not care what he said. He has been called upon by the public press to apologize for denying that statement and he has not agreed to withdraw it. He has been asked in the interests of journalism in this country to withdraw the denial because it is evident that the former prime minister told the people of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick to leave the coal in the ground. That is another question of privilege for him if he thinks he can get away with one.
He referred to the coal industry in the years from 1946 to 1956 and what his government did about the use of coal, without one coal conference and without one objection at all from those supporting the government of the day. Let me tell you this, Mr. Speaker. In 1957 through the action of this government the trend that was in progress between 1946 and 1956 was brought to a halt; and it was brought to a halt by the actions of this government. It is granted that there have been a few closures of mines in Nova Scotia, primarily because of disaster and to prevent future disasters. I refer now specifically to No. 25 colliery in my area. It was obliged to close. Otherwise more men would have lost their lives through drowning, as had happened there previously. This mine absolutely was forced to close.
He referred to the action of this government. He referred to the fact that the government announced closures. Let me for a moment come to his aid in putting across his knowledge of coal mines. I will read him a quotation from a former Liberal candidate- and I say former Liberal candidate advisedly -in the last provincial election in Nova Scotia. The quotation is that of James P. MacNeil of New Waterford. As I say, he was a candidate for the Liberal party in the last election. When this propaganda or publicity came out on the part of the government announcing closures, here is what the Liberal candidate in the last provincial election had to say about it:
Mayor James P. MacNeil of New Waterford, a miner employed In No. 16 colliery charged that the dates for closing of the mines were set by Dosco and not "by an agreement between Dosco and the government."
That is a direct quotation from one of the Liberal adherents in Nova Scotia. That is
90205-6-145
Coal Industry
the truth. It is too bad that the rest of hon. members opposite cannot get up and tell it. As I said when I rose in my place, here is a man who claims to be a coal authority. He criticizes this government for the action it has taken in preventing further closures in Cape Breton. As the indication was that January 14 was the deadline, that matter has been taken care of by this government. The unions got what they asked for at this stage. They got that date shifted back to May 31. It is my hope, and that of every other Cape Breton member, that we can bring about further delay.
The hon. member for Gloucester referred to the Rand commission report. He has indicated that he did not think it was the solution to the problem. I might say that when the last coal conference was held expressions of opinion were voiced of the Rand report. There was not one representative from Cape Breton who took objection to those representations made about the Rand report. It is only in the last couple of weeks that there has been any advocacy of adopting the Rand report. I have to agree that I did not see anything in this Rand report that was beneficial to the miners of Cape Breton, except the one problem they went into, namely the delaying of closures over a period from five to ten years. This is something with which I fully agree and I would advocate the adoption of such a plan.
Let me tell you this, Mr. Speaker, and let us get this straight. This government has offered to go further with Dosco but Dosco will not or would not accept this offer from the government. They have made up their minds. Why did not the hon. member for Gloucester get to his feet and criticize this company? Why did he not do that? He did not do it because he had no knowledge of what the situation was. Why did he not get to his feet and criticize the fact that they are closing No. 4 colliery in Glace Bay? The reason why he did not do that is that he does not know the score. He does not know what is going on in connection with coal.
The fact remains that No. 4 colliery in Glace Bay is not an uneconomical colliery. It is among the top ones, as far as economics is concerned. The company has promoted the idea that it is an uneconomical mine they are closing. That is not so. Caledonia mine in Glace Bay is an economic colliery by their own admission. What happens when you catch the company on this score is that they immediately revert to the argument that it is the quality of the coal. It is the same quality of coal that has been sold from this colliery for 60 years. Caledonia coal can be sold for 57 cents a ton less than other types. There are those companies that desire a lower quality

Coal Industry
of coal if conditions are right. That only means one thing, namely, price. Caledonia coal could be set up as a separate commodity and sold at 57 cents a ton less than the price which is an economic proposition, 57 cents a ton below the average cost.
There has been no denial at the conference by the company of this argument. Yet the executive officers see fit to feed their propaganda against me for repeating this. They did not stand behind me on that program. Neither did they stand behind me on the other argument concerning coal. They caught Mr. Albert Fairley thoroughly off base, out in left field, but they never stood behind me on that one. Yet they see fit to criticize the actions I have taken on behalf of the miners. All I can say is this. I will stand up in any public assembly and I will fire back what the absolute truth is on this situation. The miners in Caledonia are not getting the support they deserve. The hon. member for Gloucester- the coal critic of the official opposition; the man with particular knowledge of coal; the man who never attended any coal conference -gets to his feet, and what does he say? He rambles on about what somebody else said with regard to coal. He skips what his own prime minister had said about coal. He forgot that he said they should leave it in the ground. He has nothing to say about the criticism I offered to the great champion of labour from Essex East, who did not see fit to answer the correspondence I sent out on coal, but who rises in his place and tries to put himself up on a pedestal as far as the miners of Cape Breton are concerned. He did not himself have enough interest to answer a letter concerning a coal problem, and I think that if he had got together with his colleagues in the house they could have taken action that would have been beneficial to the coal miners.
With reference to the hon. member for Gloucester I am going to make a remark here which, in all fairness, I will give him an opportunity of denying. I understand that he himself has looked for an oil agency in New Brunswick, if not for himself, for somebody in his family. He is perfectly at liberty to deny that.

I should just like to wind up my remarks-there has been some delay -and refer for a moment to what the executive of the united mineworkers of America feels about the action taken by this government in delaying any action on the part of Dosco. As I have indicated, I have felt that the attitude of Dosco requires some investigation and some considerable study because it is my belief that the attitude taken by them towards the miners in Cape Breton and the community as a whole is not one which can be accepted. I myself do not for a moment accept the reasons given for closing No. 4 colliery in Glace Bay. Mr. Fairley has at times made statements in reference to this colliery and, as I have said before, not only has he been caught off base but he has been caught out in left field. He has indicated that there has been no development going on in the west side. But miners have told me that this development work is 85 per cent complete. Mr. Fairley tells me there has been no development on that side of the mine. I have on occasions reminded Mr. Fairley that this is not so. The facts are very easily proven by press releases from his own company. However, among the excuses for closing, there is the statement that no development work has been going on. I have made statements which have been severely criticized. The members of the opposition have been receiving newspaper clippings from the local paper in my constituency which severely criticize me. That is part of public life. We all have to stand up to a certain amount of criticism, and I can take it when I consider the source.
I have here a newspaper clipping whose heading says: "Marsh, Dolhanty, say Statements are Inaccurate". They are the president and vice president of UMW District 26. I am a member of the union, a member of the Caledonia Local, a paid up member. The clipping is here for everybody to see, and I face up to the situation every time. They go so far as to say my statements were immoral, and when they say that they are referring to a remark I made at Sydney when I said that 800 miners at Caledonia colliery were not getting the support from their union executive that they could rightfully expect. This is the statement that brought on all the criticism. They say it was immoral. I went on to say I thought the union executive would be satisfied with fewer contented miners rather than a large number of discontented miners. This was the statement they referred to as being immoral. Yet I pointed out clearly that this was exactly the practice followed

by John L. Lewis, formerly president of the union in the United States. He advocated the closing of uneconomic mines. Strictly on a business level that idea might have merit. It does not have merit when applied to the Caledonia colliery at Glace Bay because that colliery is economical. Anybody who withdraws from the argument because of that consideration is withdrawing from the truth. It can easily be proven, but this is one portion of the argument which the union has failed to put forward on behalf of the miners of No. 4 colliery.
Now I should like to call the attention of the house to what the executive members of the UMW think of the action taken by this government. In criticizing me, Mr. Dolhanty says:
I only hope that he is not voicing government policy. We have worked very closely with both the provincial and federal governments over the years. They have given us much help.
I have placed on the record what the UMW executive has said about this government. They have worked very closely together and this government has given them very much help. Those are the words of vice president Dolhanty. There they are in black and white.
I notice that the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) is finally back in his seat. That hon. gentleman saw fit to rise in this house and ask direct questions of the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys. The hon. member is very seriously concerned about the situation in Cape Breton, so seriously concerned that he failed to answer a letter I sent to him on behalf of these same miners. So seriously concerned with this matter is the hon. gentleman that I have never seen anything that he has said that takes opposition to the policy enunciated by the former leader of his party and then prime minister of Canada. I will remind him what the former prime minister said. Since the hon. member is late in arriving, I will repeat it for his benefit. The former prime minister said, in effect, leave the coal in the ground for future generations so they can manufacture synthetic articles.
One of the hon. member's colleagues took exception to this and has been severely criticized editorially for so doing.
It is my hope and I am sure it is the hope of every hon. member from Cape Breton and Nova Scotia that the closing down of mines in Nova Scotia and Cape Breton can be further delayed. I might say that the action taken by this government has had the effect of continually setting back this date. Attempts have been made for some considerable time to close the mines. A trend of closing mines gained impetus from 1946 to

1956. This government brought that trend to a halt. Regardless of what is said by hon. members of the opposition, this government is the only government that has taken a genuine interest in the miners of Nova Scotia.
The very determined effort on the part of Dosco to close out No. 4 colliery on January 14, has again been delayed to May 31. It is my hope that something will develop between now and that date which will bring about a further delay of these proposed shutdowns.
I wish now to speak briefly about the so-called new party. Apparently it operates under the delusion that it is going to be the saviour of the Cape Breton miner. The new party has a certain element of the Cape Breton miners believing that this new party is capable of saving the industry. I do not know how beneficial the new party will be, but I remind the Cape Breton miners that there is no hope of salvation to be found in the new party. I think there is very little hope of the new party finding itself elected anywhere. As far as I can see personally, it is simply not going to go over. In fact, I draw that conclusion from some of the remarks that have been made from time to time by hon. members down in the corner of the chamber.
I do not mean to hurt the feelings of the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue). I have been given to understand through the press and other media that the man who could have the leadership of the so-called new party merely by snapping his fingers is Mr. Douglas. All that is required, apparently is that he accept the leadership of the so-called new party. I do not really get the drift of this matter. They were labour, they became the C.C.F. and now they are merging with labour and farmers to become the new party. I hope they get the name straightened out before too long so we will know exactly what they are.
